correctness.rationale: Every directed wheel orientation is partitioned by its spoke word. Mixed spoke words require exactly B-to-A boundary rim arcs, giving an even number of runs and acyclicity. Reversibility is proved via alternative directed paths: all boundary rim arcs are nonflippable, within-run rim arcs are flippable, and spokes are flippable exactly at sources/sinks of internally oriented path runs. The path-source polynomial follows from exact virtual-boundary sign-change counting, yielding the rational run generating function. Constant spokes require a separately proved one-minority-rim correction. Summing cyclic compositions gives the displayed degree polynomial with all normalizations (2m/k) accounted for. The Lucas formula follows by a factored logarithmic generating function. Minimum and maximum degree bounds are sharp for every m>=3; m=3 is isolated explicitly. Independent direct all-orientation DAG/reachability enumeration for m=3..8 and algebraic/composition checks for m=3..12 passed, while the symbolic proof covers all m.

originality.rationale: The claimed new assertion is a full local-degree polynomial for the wheel acyclic-orientation flip graph, with Lucas-number simple-vertex enumeration and exact maximum-degree multiplicities. Savage--Squire--West (1993) establish the same acyclic orientation objects, their spoke/rim constraints, cardinality, and Hamiltonian properties, but do not state the local-degree profile. Grujic (2016) derives global f-polynomials of graphical zonotopes, which determine the total edge count but do not determine vertex-degree multiplicities. Earlier reported degree results for complete bipartite and split graph orientation spaces, and wheel spanning-tree exchange spaces, concern different graphs or states and do not imply this wheel orientation degree profile. Semantic archive and primary-literature searches produced no equivalent/covering statement. value.rationale: A wheel is a canonical planar nonchordal family whose acyclic-orientation flip graph already featured prominently in the 1993 Gray-code literature. A complete local degree polynomial gives all transformation branching counts, far finer than the known total number of states and global f-vector. The nontrivial Lucas-number formula counts exactly the simple vertices of the corresponding graphical zonotope, and proves their proportion decays exponentially. Sharp maximal degree and multiplicities add an exact all-size local extremal classification. This is a natural combinatorial gap, not an arbitrary small parameter slice or a recomputation of a known global count.
